title: Studio, freelancer, or in-house for a first serious site
excerpt: Use a freelancer for one narrow skill, hire in-house when the work never stops, and bring in a studio when a defined launch needs design and production code together.
alt: Five people working on laptops around a wooden table. The table is the practical question: how many roles you need in the room for a first serious site.
caption: The shape of the team is the decision. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: When is a freelancer the right hire for a site?
faqs.answer: Hire a freelancer when the job is one skill you can describe: a logo, a set of pages in an existing system, or a front-end pass on a design you already trust. You still own direction, review, and whatever skill they do not cover. If design and build both need inventing, a single freelancer is being asked to be a studio.

faqs.question: When should the first site be an in-house hire?
faqs.answer: Hire in-house when the site or product will change every week and you want that person in the company. Budget the time to recruit, manage, and cover the skills they do not have. A first marketing site with a clear edge is usually a project, not a headcount decision.

faqs.question: What does a studio do that the other two shapes do not?
faqs.answer: A studio brings design and production code together for a launch you can name. You get a small team that can hold brand, interface, and the repository at once, then hand the result back. You do not get a permanent department, and you should not expect them to invent the business.

markdown:
The design agency vs freelancer choice is really three shapes. Use a freelancer for a narrow skill. Hire in-house when the work never stops. Use a studio when a defined launch needs design and build together.

A first serious site is the usual moment this comes up. The company has outgrown a template, the offer is real, and someone has to make a public page a stranger can understand. The right shape depends on how wide the skill is, and whether the work has an edge.

## A freelancer for a narrow skill

A freelancer is the right person when you can point at the task. A wordmark. A set of illustrations. A front end from a design that is already decided. A migration script. One craft, a clear done, a start and a finish.

You remain the integrator. If the freelancer designs and someone else must build, you are the person who keeps the type, the content, and the components from drifting apart. That is fine when you have the judgment and the time. It is expensive when you are also selling, supporting, and writing the offer.

Be precise in the brief. A freelancer engaged as “make the site” will either shrink the job to what they do best or stretch into work they do not want to own. Neither outcome is a quarrel. It is a fuzzy edge. Name the pages, the states, and what they will hand back: files, a repository, or both.

The risk on a first serious site is coverage. Brand, interface, front-end code, content structure, and launch mechanics rarely live in one independent. If you hire one person to cover all of them, you have hired a studio of one, without the backup when they are ill or booked. Sometimes that person is extraordinary. Plan as if they are a specialist, and add the missing skill on purpose.

## In-house when the work never stops

Hire an employee when the site or the product will keep changing after launch, and you want that judgment inside the company. A designer who sits with support every day will see different problems than a studio that returns for a phase. An engineer on the team will live with the repository.

The cost is time before any page exists. Recruiting, managing, and equipping a hire is its own project. A single in-house designer still needs engineering if you want a production site. A single in-house engineer still needs design direction if you care how the company looks. One hire does not close the gap unless their craft matches the gap you actually have.

In-house is the right default when the product is the company and the interface will be in motion for years. It is a heavy default for a marketing site you will edit, not reinvent, each month. You can hire after the first launch, once you know which skill you are tired of renting. Many founders do this in that order: a studio for the first serious public site, then a hire when the edits become a job.

Ownership still matters. An employee should work in accounts the company controls. A studio should too. The difference is presence, not a license to keep the domain in someone else’s email.

## A studio when design and build share a date

A studio is the right shape when the launch needs both disciplines and you can describe the edge. Home, a product or service page, proof, a way to start a conversation. Or a shop with a catalog, a product page, and checkout. Or a focused product interface with one workflow polished, including the empty and error states.

Hanabi is this shape: a product design and web development studio for founders and small teams. The work is interface design, production front ends, brand systems, ecommerce, and the occasional specific automation. Design and code stay in one place so the brand and the interface can share an idea. The tools are ordinary and ownable: Figma for the design, Next.js, React, and TypeScript in a repository you keep.

You are not hiring a large bench, and you should not be. A small team that does the work it shows is the point. Ask who will be on the project. Ask what you will own. Ask what happens to a change request once the date is set. Those questions separate a studio engagement from a retainer you did not mean to start, and from a freelance arrangement that quietly needed a second and third person.

A studio is the wrong shape when you want someone in the office every day, or when the task is smaller than a launch. Paying a studio to tweak a banner is a mismatch. So is asking a studio to become your product department without saying so. If the idea is still too loose to name a first slice, scope that slice before you pick the shape. The contract cannot invent the offer.

## The quality bar does not change with the shape

Whoever builds the first serious site, the page still has to be readable, operable, and honest. The W3C’s [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) organize that bar into four ideas: perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. You do not need a certification speech from a freelancer, an employee, or a studio. You do need contrast that holds, focus that shows, names on controls, and text that says what the company does.

Put that in the brief no matter which shape you choose. A beautiful desktop frame that fails on a phone, or a clever motion that ignores reduced motion, is not finished. The shape of the team does not relax the standard. It only changes who is in the room when the standard is applied.

Speed belongs in the same conversation. A first site that looks finished and loads in a way you would not send to a customer is not the serious site you asked for. Ask each kind of partner how they will keep the page fast. The answer should mention images, type, and how the page is built, not a plugin name alone.

## A way to decide this month

Write two sentences. What has to be true on the launch date? Will someone inside the company keep changing it every week after that?

If the task is one skill and you can review it, hire the freelancer. If the work is continuous and you are ready to manage, open the in-house role. If the launch needs design and code together, and you can name the pages, talk to a studio.

You can mix them later. A studio launch plus a freelancer for photography is a common pair. An in-house marketer plus a studio for the rebuild is another. The mistake is mixing them on day one without an owner. Someone has to accept the page. Name that person before the first invoice.

Once you know you want a studio, the next decision is how to choose among them. That piece is [how to hire a design and development studio](/blog/how-to-hire-a-design-studio).
